item.title: Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon
item.description:
How Meta's Reality Labs brought Cuttlefish and its QEMU backend to macOS and Apple silicon. [...]

Read More...

The post Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
item.content:encoded:
Meta’s Reality Labs builds products such as AI glasses. Emulators provide us with a way to scale development and testing without relying on scarce physical hardware.

Testing software for non-phone Android devices depends on how closely a virtual device reproduces the software behavior of the physical product. While a lightweight emulator like Goldfish gets you part of the way, differences from the real device can hide bugs until later in development. This lack of fidelity also erodes trust in device emulation, increasing reliance on scarce physical hardware.

Cuttlefish is the Android Open Source Project’s (AOSP’s) virtual-device framework for testing Android software against virtual hardware. It boots the same system images as real hardware and runs a realistic software stack against virtual hardware. This enables Cuttlefish to more closely track a physical device’s behavior than a lightweight emulator does.

Unfortunately, Cuttlefish is only supported on Linux, and our application and library developers work on Macs with Apple silicon. This forced us to support Goldfish and Cuttlefish side by side.

We knew if we could consolidate onto a single Cuttlefish-based platform, we could give all of our developers the benefit of the same high-fidelity virtual device. The challenge was porting the stack to make Cuttlefish run natively on macOS.

The Impact of Fragmentation

Maintaining dual emulator platforms imposed a heavy operational burden: It drained computing resources, created confusion for developers, and slowed down the emulator team. Every tool required support for two separate platforms, while infrastructure and engineering capacity were divided between them. Furthermore, developers had to choose an emulator target based on how they worked: Goldfish ran everywhere but had less fidelity while Cuttlefish needed Linux.

The AOSP mirrors this exact divide: Goldfish targets application developers, whereas Cuttlefish serves Android platform developers. So long as we maintained that division, we would suffer the effects of fragmentation.

The Stack and the macOS Gaps

Cuttlefish is the orchestration layer, while the component that actually runs the guest OS is a virtual machine monitor (VMM). On Linux, Cuttlefish normally uses crosvm but previously included support for QEMU as an alternative VMM. That integration had become inactive over time. To enable native Apple silicon support on macOS, we revived QEMU support.

Many of Cuttlefish’s virtual devices use vhost-user backends, separate processes that provide virtio devices to QEMU over a socket. The architecture is clean, but large parts of it were written with a hard Linux assumption. Three of those assumptions break on macOS. The vhost-user machinery is gated to Linux and won’t build or run. The Apple hypervisor imposes resource limits QEMU didn’t expect. Finally, the native display, build, and signing paths didn’t exist. We tackled all three.

Making vhost-user Portable Beyond Linux

The most structurally important changes were in QEMU’s vhost-user path. The frontends, libvhost-user, and the contrib backends such as vhost-user-blk were all gated to Linux. We relaxed those build restrictions so the vhost-user frontends and libraries can build on macOS as well as Linux. This lets Cuttlefish’s device backends hand off to QEMU on a Mac the same way they do on Linux. Without this, the higher-fidelity device model that makes Cuttlefish worth using isn’t available outside Linux.

Living Within Hypervisor.framework

On Apple silicon, QEMU accelerates through HVF (Hypervisor.framework) instead of KVM. QEMU’s HVF backend did not track enough memory regions for larger Cuttlefish configurations. We increased its tracking-slot count so those configurations could run correctly.

A Usable Native Display

Local application development requires an interactive display allowing developers to view and engage directly with the virtual device. To enable direct interaction and bypass reliance on the WebRTC interface, we transitioned to QEMU’s native Cocoa display. The changes include:

  • BGRA Pixel Format Support: Enables accurate display rendering to eliminate visual artifacts on Apple silicon.
  • Mouse-Click-as-Touch: Translates pointer actions into touch input for interacting with touchscreen devices.
  • Custom Geometry Options: Adds the -g flag to graphic_console_init for display configuration.

We also enabled the unstable Rutabaga structs needed to match the Rust-side graphics ABI in gfxstream/rutabaga configurations.

Building and Signing on Apple Silicon

Finally, there was the build and packaging work: initial Darwin build support, building QEMU for arm64 on macOS, and toolchain fixes. The macOS builds also needed the JIT entitlement in addition to support for code signing and notarization. On the Cuttlefish side, we added macOS host support so the framework’s orchestration builds and runs on a Mac instead of assuming a Linux host.

The Benefits

By moving to a unified platform, we cut maintenance requirements, reduced infrastructure needs, eliminated redundant tooling, enhanced fidelity, and ensured developers run the exact same Cuttlefish virtual devices used across CI.

A single platform also made it easier to support capabilities on a shared stack, including:

  • Bluetooth pairing and connectivity.
  • Wi-Fi.
  • Cellular.
  • 3D graphics.
  • Over-the-air (OTA) update testing to exercise over-the-air update flows against a virtual device.
  • Fastboot.
  • Snapshotting to save and restore device state in CI and development flows.

Beyond supporting Reality Labs engineers, this identical virtual device is shared with external developers building for our ecosystem. This alignment guarantees that third-party teams test against the exact same Cuttlefish-based platform we use to develop and validate the OS itself.

With AI agents playing a growing role in Android development, validation execution and runtime behavior is just as essential as code generation. Virtual devices empower both engineers and automated agents to operate concurrently within isolated environments, facilitating application execution and rapid iteration. By enabling instant state resets and repeated test runs, teams eliminate dependencies on shared physical hardware and prevent workflow interruptions. Ultimately, high-fidelity emulation ensures these continuous feedback loops are both rapid and meaningful.

Giving Back to the Community

Although we built this for development within Reality Labs, the macOS support is useful beyond our products. We’re sharing our work with the community so other developers can build on the QEMU and AOSP foundations that enabled our work.

We’re distributing the work in two parts:

  • qemu-wearables: a Meta-maintained fork of QEMU carrying our commits.
  • cuttlefish-wearables: a set of patch files, with instructions for patching Android/AOSP.

The repositories contain our QEMU changes and the Cuttlefish patch series, along with build and patch-application instructions.

We’re also exploring ways to contribute these changes upstream to QEMU and AOSP. In the meantime, developers can use our fork and patch set.

Acknowledgements

This project relies on the foundations laid by the QEMU and Cuttlefish/AOSP communities. We are particularly grateful for the vsock-user implementation created by Stefano Garzarella, which directly enabled our macOS integration.

Special thanks also go to Olya Arkhangelskaia and Tom Care at Meta for their foundational work bringing Cuttlefish to macOS, and to Jeffrey Effendy for improvements to the native Mac developer experience and subsequent productization work.

The post Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon appeared first on Engineering at Meta.

item.title: Your Algorithm: Giving People More Ways to Personalize Facebook Recommendations
item.description:
Your algorithm is a suite of AI-powered tools that makes Facebook recommendations more transparent and steerable, with a single editable view of the interests that shape Feed and Reels. The post Your Algorithm: Giving People More Ways to Personalize Facebook Recommendations appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
item.content:encoded:
• Your algorithm is a suite of AI-powered tools that makes Facebook recommendations more transparent and steerable, with a single editable view of the interests that shape Feed and Reels.
  • We’re sharing how Your algorithm turns people’s natural language preferences into responsive recommendations, and how LLMs are tailored to specific tasks within the system.

Traditionally, the recommendation systems behind what people see on Facebook have learned from implicit engagement signals. While this allows them to scale well, it also means they adapt slowly and capture little nuance. But what if people could interact directly with the algorithms that rank and recommend what they see to instantly make their recommendations more personal and customized?

Your algorithm is an end-to-end system that addresses the limitations of adaptability and nuance in recommendations. This new suite of AI-powered tools lets people on Facebook state, in their own words, what they want to see in their Feed and Reels. By tasking a collection of large language models (LLMs) with understanding, storing, and tracking people’s stated preferences along with their user behavior, we’ve created a recommendation system that responds to people’s preferences and adjusts the content they see.

An Overview of the Your Algorithm System Architecture

The Your algorithm page has three parts (Figure 1): 

  • At the top, a one-sentence Lately Summary that describes recent viewing activity. 
  • Below it are two lists: 
    • “Interested In,” prefilled with interests inferred from past activity. 
    • “Not Interested In,” capturing topics the user has explicitly marked as not interested, or has X-ed out or hidden on Facebook. 

People can use the interface to add interests (using natural language), move them between lists, or remove them. Every change applies responsively to both Feed and Reels, and will further update as the person gives feedback on individual posts. 

Your algorithm system has several components that cover the full lifecycle of a preference, from inferring and validating it to applying it in ranking and delivery (Figure 2). 

  • Profile generation builds the initial interest profile.
  • Preference management validates each change, enriches it with the signals ranking needs, and saves it to a single store that both Feed and Reels read, ensuring that the preferences shown on the page are the same ones used in ranking. 
  • Ranking applies the “Interested In” and “Not Interested In” lists throughout the funnel. 
  • Delivery optimization helps each change take effect more responsively.

From Preferences Into Recommendations

Turning a stated preference into recommendations poses three distinct problems. An interest added to Interested In needs to deliver relevant content quickly, without crowding out everything else. An interest added to Not Interested In needs to hold reliably, even though topics are fuzzy and any single filter misses some matches. And both need to take effect responsively, even when the next recommendations were cached before the change.

Your algorithm addresses each problem with dedicated logic across the recommendation funnel, from retrieval through reranking to the device (Figure 3).

Interested In: Surfacing New Interests Without Flooding

Each interest in Interested In drives four dedicated retrieval sources. Two find matching content directly (through search and through clusters of closely related topics), and two extend reach through the content graph and item-to-item similarity. Retrieving explicitly for each interest ensures enough relevant candidates for downstream ranking. 

This is important because, without it, content about a brand-new interest might never enter the ranking pipeline at all. Candidates that pass a relevance check, which compares the meaning of the interest with each candidate, receive a promotion in late-stage ranking so they can compete alongside other content. A control layer in reranking then determines where they appear.

Responsiveness alone is not the goal. Our approach emphasizes balance over volume: A new interest should show up, not take over. The control layer spaces out recommendations for the same interest and caps each interest’s daily contribution. Retrieval also fetches candidates for only one interest per request, so every interest gets a turn. New interests receive extra weight for a limited period. After that, the recommendation system learns from how people engage with that content.

Not Interested In: Layered Filtering at Every Stage

Interests in Not Interested In are enforced at several stages based on different signals to achieve high precision and recall. During ranking, the same embedding-based comparison used in the relevance check removes candidates too close to an interest in Not Interested In, and demotion rules push down near matches. After ranking, the LLM reranker reviews the final list. On the device, cache invalidation, described below, removes matching candidates that are already queued for display.

Not every entry in Not Interested In is about a topic. Quality-related requests, such as reducing AI-generated or sexually suggestive content, map to dedicated demotion signals rather than topic matching. When a request names a creator, that creator’s content is filtered out directly.

Responsiveness Optimization

Even with ranking tuned to respond to preferences, there is still room to improve how responsively a change reaches what people see. Content for a new preference is not picked up until the next fetch request, and content already cached on the device was ranked before the preference was set. 

We added two delivery mechanisms to close these gaps. When a new interest is added to Interested In, the system sends an extra fetch request outside the normal fetch cycle, called a supplementary tail load, to retrieve fresh recommendations so matching content appears quickly. When an interest is added to Not Interested In, cache invalidation handles candidates ranked before the change. The client obtains the new interest’s clusters and drops any cached content that matches them before it is displayed.

LLMs Across the Preference Lifecycle: From Profile to Final Check

LLMs play a role at several key points in a preference’s life in Your algorithm. They generate the initial profile that people see on a first visit, validate each change as it is made, and give the final recommendations a last check against interests in Not Interested In (Figure 2). Each use comes with its own constraints, including latency, serving capacity, and safety, and evaluating them requires a new approach as well.

Profile generation provides the starting content for a first visit: the inferred interests and the Lately Summary. An LLM turns interest signals, which are refreshed regularly, into a set of inferred interests with clear, readable topic names. These are prefilled in the Interested In list and reflect past viewing across Facebook Feed and Reels. The LLM also writes the Lately Summary, a sentence that highlights ongoing interests. Together, they provide a recognizable starting point that is easy to review and correct.

Every edit on the Your algorithm page passes through preference management. When an interest is added or moved, an LLM checks that the phrase is a coherent topic, detects duplicates, and maps it to a clean topic name. This step runs on a smaller model that is efficient to serve at scale. The validated interest is then enriched with the signals ranking needs, such as an embedding and search keywords, and saved to the shared preference store. The LLM is only one layer of validation. The system also has a dedicated component that performs integrity and safety checks. 

Once recommendations are ranked, LLM reranking provides a last check against interests in Not Interested In. The ranking funnel matches interests to candidates using embeddings, which are fast but coarse. To catch what they miss, a fine-tuned LLM reviews the ranked list and removes content it judges to be related to an interest recently added to Not Interested In. A key insight was that a small model fine-tuned to return only the items to remove was faster and more reliable than a general-purpose model judging each item individually.

Evaluating these LLM calls required its own approach. Standard offline metrics cannot tell whether a Lately Summary is accurate or whether the reranker removed the right candidates, so a separate LLM acts as a judge, grading each call’s output against expected behavior. This provides an objective, repeatable way to compare prompts and models before launch.

The Future of Your Algorithm

Your algorithm creates a more transparent and personalized recommendation experience, informed by both behavior and stated intent. But there are important opportunities remaining, such as better interpreting ambiguous input and making recommendations respond even more precisely to each request. We are also exploring additional entry points so that preferences can be shaped from more places.

Acknowledgments

This work reflects critical contributions from a cross-functional v-team across Meta (in alphabetical order):

Adi Gupta, Aryan Porwal, Bernabe Soto, Chao Yang, Chen Chen, Chen Kovacs, Chengxi Li, Chih-Wei Chang, Clare Yip, Cuong Nguyen, Dahni Ma, Daniel Thiyagu, Danny Kanoff, David Yuan, Devin Ding, Devon Pan, Eric Landgrebe, Feng Zhang, George Lu, Grace Yang, Hai-Son Dang, Haisen Hong, Hongyi Shi, Hongyi Wu, Howard Lu, Huijun Qian, Igor Vodov, Iordanis Fostiropoulos, Jakara Mato, Jasmine Neisser, Jason Liu, Jason Song, Jean-Pascal Billaud, Jeffrey Lin, Jeffrey Santelli, Jian Chen, Jianyu Wang, Jiaye Pan, Jinho Hwang, Joe Sena, Jordan Reich, Kanghua Wu, Khoi Pham, Kim Trang Leaf, Kris Katsanevas, Kuo-Feng Hsu, Kushal Adhvaryu, Liyu Wang, Manish Khettry, Matthew Miao, Mayoor Rai, Momo Jiao, Nakul Tirumalai, Patrick Boocock, Patrick Cullen, Qi Guo, Qichao Que, Queenie Li, Ratish Nair, Sanyogeeta Lawande, Satvik Eltepu, Sean Chen, Shijie Xie, Shuai Zhang, Shuoyan Yin, Smruthi Gowtham, Tsung-Yi Huang, Tyler Pell, Wanting Jiang, Wanyu Li, Weiwei Jiang, Xiangyu Xu, Xin Wang, Xinyang Feng, Yanchen Wang, Yibo Zhu, Yihao Li, Yihui Saw, Yinjie Huang, Yu-Wei Wu, Yuchen Shao, Yue Wang, Yue Zhang, Yuhan Yang, Yuqi Shen, Zhen Hang Jiang, Zhiyu Liu, Zhongwei Teng, Zijiang Yang, Zoe Zu

item.title: Extending LLDB to Debug Applications That Span CPUs and GPUs
item.description:
We built a vendor-neutral accelerator plugin architecture in lldb-server for debugging applications that span CPUs and GPUs. It separates shared debugger infrastructure from hardware-specific device control. The design represents the CPU and GPU as separate debugger processes while presenting them in one debugging session. Modern AI applications rarely execute in one place. A workload can [...]

Read More...

The post Extending LLDB to Debug Applications That Span CPUs and GPUs appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
item.content:encoded:
• We built a vendor-neutral accelerator plugin architecture in lldb-server for debugging applications that span CPUs and GPUs. It separates shared debugger infrastructure from hardware-specific device control.
  • The design represents the CPU and GPU as separate debugger processes while presenting them in one debugging session.

Modern AI applications rarely execute in one place. A workload can begin in a high-level framework and move back and forth between native CPU code and kernels running on a GPU. When a bug crosses those boundaries, developers need to understand the host application and the device together.

That is harder than attaching a conventional debugger to another process. The CPU and GPU may use different instruction sets, registers, memory spaces, and execution models. The GPU is also controlled through a runtime and driver inside the host process, so debugging the device often requires careful coordination with the CPU.

Historically, GPU vendors built device-specific debuggers, including AMD’s ROCgdb and NVIDIA’s CUDA-GDB. These tools provide deep support for their respective platforms, but common debugger capabilities must often be implemented and maintained separately.

At Meta, we have been developing a different approach for LLDB: a common accelerator plugin architecture in lldb-server. In this post, “GPU” refers to the concrete devices and examples, while “accelerator” refers to LLDB’s broader, vendor-neutral plugin abstraction. The architecture has evolved through contributions from engineers at Meta and across the accelerator ecosystem. It keeps the shared debugger independent of any one GPU while giving hardware vendors a focused place to implement device-specific behavior.

Why GPU Debugging Challenges Traditional Debugger Models

A traditional debugger generally assumes that one process has one architecture and a consistent view of threads, registers, and memory. GPU programs challenge each of those assumptions.

A host process might run on x86-64 while its kernels use a completely different instruction set. A CPU thread has a familiar register context, while a GPU may execute groups of lanes in lockstep. Host and device pointers can refer to different address spaces. A GPU can expose thousands of execution lanes, which do not map cleanly onto the thread model that most command-line and graphical debuggers present.

Combining all of this state into one artificial process model makes the debugger more complicated. Every operation must first determine whether it applies to the CPU or the GPU. Register handling, memory reads, breakpoints, stepping, and stop events all become conditional on the selected hardware. A single process model also forces the CPU and GPU into one unified memory map, even though their address spaces can be independent: The same address, such as 0x1000, can refer to different locations in the CPU and GPU processes.

Instead of hiding those differences, the LLDB accelerator architecture gives them a clear boundary.

Plugin Support in lldb-server for GPU Debugging

LLDB uses a companion process called lldb-server to launch or attach to a program and perform low-level debugging operations. The LLDB client communicates with the server through the GDB remote protocol, a command protocol for operations such as reading memory, inspecting registers, controlling execution, and setting breakpoints.

Because lldb-server already controls the native process, it is also the right place to coordinate with an accelerator runtime. The new plugin interface lets a hardware-specific backend work alongside the normal CPU debugger. The backend translates a vendor’s device debugging API into concepts LLDB already understands, such as processes, threads, registers, memory, modules, and stop reasons.

This separation keeps the LLDB client vendor-neutral. Common improvements to the command line, remote protocol, symbol handling, and IDE integration can benefit every accelerator. At the same time, each vendor remains responsible for the details that are unique to its hardware and driver stack.

GPU debugging support is activated only when the debugged application uses a supported GPU runtime. For CPU-only applications, LLDB and lldb-server continue through the existing native debugging path without incurring runtime computational overhead.

Two Targets, One Debugging Experience

The architecture represents the CPU and accelerator as separate LLDB targets.
Each target has its own architecture and is associated with a debugger process that maintains its threads, registers, address space, and execution state. The CPU continues to use LLDB’s established native debugging path. When the accelerator becomes available, the plugin provides a second connection that LLDB uses to create the device target.

To the debugger, the two targets remain technically independent. To the developer, they can appear in one LLDB or IDE session. This avoids forcing incompatible CPU and GPU concepts into a single process while still supporting a unified workflow.

Coordinating the Host and Device

A typical debugging session follows a small set of steps:

  1. LLDB connects to lldb-server and discovers which accelerator plugins are available.
  2. A plugin can ask LLDB to set internal breakpoints in the host process. These breakpoints identify important runtime events, such as the point at which a GPU debugging session can begin.
  3. When the host reaches one of those points, lldb-server notifies the plugin. The plugin initializes the vendor debugging API and prepares an accelerator debugging endpoint.
  4. LLDB creates a second target for the accelerator and connects to it. Device threads, registers, memory, modules, and breakpoints can then use LLDB’s existing abstractions.

Structured actions coordinate the two sides. A plugin can request CPU breakpoints, provide connection information, report device modules, and synchronize host and device execution. The common protocol describes what the debugger needs to do without exposing vendor-specific API details to the LLDB client.

We also built a mock accelerator plugin that exercises this flow without specialized hardware. It lets the LLVM test suite verify discovery, breakpoint coordination, connection creation, and basic device state. This has been important for developing shared infrastructure that can be reviewed and tested independently of any particular GPU.

A Typical GPU Workflow

The vector dot-product HIP sample produced this abridged session:

(lldb) target list
Current targets:
  target #0: gpu_demo (x86_64, stopped)
* target #1: amd_memory_kernel[...] (amdgcn, stopped)

(lldb) b compute_element
Breakpoint 1: no locations (pending).
(lldb) c
(lldb) target select 0
(lldb) c
Launching kernel: 2 blocks x 32 threads
1 location added to breakpoint 1
Target 1 stopped.

(lldb) target select 1
(lldb) bt
* frame #0: compute_element(..., idx=32) at gpu_demo.hip:26
  frame #1: vector_dot_kernel(..., n=64) at gpu_demo.hip:35
The pending breakpoint resolves when the GPU module loads, and the backtrace
comes from the GPU target.

A Common Plugin Framework Across Hardware Vendors

The plugin boundary is intentionally based on debugger operations rather than concepts from a specific GPU platform. That makes it useful across devices with very different instruction sets, runtime APIs, and execution models.

The framework supports postmortem GPU debugging as well as live sessions. GPU core-dump plugins use a common base class for their LLDB integration, while vendor implementations provide the device-specific thread, register, memory, and module state.

GPU debugging efforts at Meta are already leveraging the architecture. Because we operate a heterogeneous fleet of GPUs with different hardware and software stacks, the fact that these efforts use the same model is an important validation of the design: the common LLDB layer can remain stable while each backend represents its own device accurately.

At the time of writing, we have upstreamed most of the common framework to LLVM. This includes the lldb-server plugin interface; GDB-remote packets for plugin discovery, initialization, runtime-event coordination, and GPU connection creation; support for associating CPU and GPU debugger processes while preserving their independent architecture; support for multiple address spaces, and hardware-independent mock tests. We expect to upstream the remaining pieces soon.

Looking Ahead

Next, we plan to finish upstreaming the remaining common infrastructure and expand the vendor integrations built on it. Our goal is that integrating new hardware with LLDB should require only a vendor-specific plugin, not a separate debugger to build and maintain. 

Acknowledgements 

We are grateful to Meta’s Developer Infrastructure leadership team, especially Shane Nay, Todd Fiala, and Ale Contenti, whose direct support made this work possible.

We also thank our Debugging & Tooling teammates Jacob Lalonde, David Young, Alexandre Perez, Zhiyuan Li, Piyush Jaiswal, and Philip DePetro for their collaboration and support.

Finally, we thank the open source community, especially Jonas Devlieghere, Jim Ingham, David Spickett, and Jason Molenda, for reviewing the RFCs and upstream pull requests.
